neurips-2013-variational-inference-for-m.tldr: Variational inference accounts for uncertainty in Gaussian-process distance metrics.
paragraphs: Gaussian process regression depends on a kernel that determines which inputs should count as similar. Parameters such as length scales control that judgment, and the paper asks how to account for uncertainty in these parameters instead of treating a single fitted setting as settled.

The authors introduce a variational approximation that approximately integrates out kernel hyperparameters. Their construction adapts a variational framework developed for Gaussian process latent variable models and combines it with a standardized representation of the Gaussian process. They apply the method specifically to learning Mahalanobis distance metrics for regression.

Experiments compare the approach with existing methods on datasets with high-dimensional inputs. The abstract does not provide numerical results or identify a consistent winner, so its supported contribution is the inference method and its evaluation in this setting. The central idea is to make uncertainty about input geometry part of the regression calculation.

neurips-2014-efficient-sampling-for-lear.tldr: Sparse additive functions can be recovered efficiently from carefully chosen noisy queries.
paragraphs: The paper studies a function of many input coordinates whose value is actually the sum of smooth functions of only a few coordinates. Both the relevant coordinates and their individual contributions are unknown. The objective is to reconstruct each contribution uniformly, using queries that return function values at chosen inputs.

The authors specify sampling points and a randomized recovery algorithm. Their method combines compressive sensing with a new convex quadratic program for approximating one-dimensional functions. This recovery step can tolerate query errors that are arbitrary but bounded, rather than requiring every observation to be exact.

The results are theoretical: the paper establishes sample-complexity bounds and analyzes both bounded and stochastic noise. Its guarantees depend on the sparse additive structure and smoothness assumptions. This makes the work a study of when high-dimensional function learning can exploit a small number of active coordinates, rather than a claim about unrestricted functions.

neurips-2014-generative-adversarial-nets.tldr: A generator learns by competing with a discriminator that identifies generated samples.
paragraphs: Learning to generate data requires a way to judge whether synthetic examples resemble the training distribution. This paper proposes doing that through two models trained together: a generator G produces examples, while a discriminator D estimates whether an example came from the training data or from G.

The generator is trained to make the discriminator wrong, producing a minimax game between the two models. For unrestricted functions, the authors identify a unique solution in which G recovers the training distribution and D assigns probability 1/2 everywhere. With multilayer perceptrons, the system can be trained using backpropagation.

The framework avoids Markov chains and unrolled approximate inference networks during both training and sample generation. Qualitative and quantitative experiments demonstrate its potential. The equilibrium result concerns the unrestricted-function setting; the abstract does not establish that practical neural-network training always reaches that solution. Its contribution is a new adversarial formulation of generative learning.

neurips-2014-optimization-methods-for-sp.tldr: Proximal-gradient optimization accelerates sparse graphical-model estimation with CONCORD.
paragraphs: Sparse graphical models describe relationships among many variables while retaining relatively few connections. Existing scalable optimization techniques often assume a Gaussian model. CONCORD instead uses a convex regression-based pseudo-likelihood for estimating partial-correlation graphs, but its original coordinate-wise optimization leaves room for faster computational methods.

The authors introduce CONCORD-ISTA and CONCORD-FISTA, two proximal-gradient algorithms for the corresponding l1-regularized inverse-covariance estimation problem. These methods bring established convex-optimization machinery into the pseudo-likelihood framework, where the statistical formulation can operate beyond the Gaussian functional form.

Timing comparisons with cyclic coordinate-wise minimization show substantial computational gains, and the paper proves convergence and convergence rates. The abstract characterizes the resulting approach as highly scalable but supplies no particular runtime or dataset size. The contribution is therefore both algorithmic and theoretical: faster optimization for this estimator, accompanied by guarantees that the optimization procedure converges.

neurips-2014-projective-dictionary-pair-.tldr: Learning analysis and synthesis dictionaries together makes discriminative dictionary learning faster.
paragraphs: Dictionary-learning classifiers represent an input using learned building blocks and try to make that representation useful for distinguishing classes. Many approaches impose l0 or l1 sparsity constraints on the representation coefficients. Solving for those coefficients can make both model training and classification computationally expensive.

This paper proposes projective dictionary pair learning, or DPL. It jointly learns a synthesis dictionary for representing signals and an analysis dictionary, organizing the representation and discrimination objectives within one framework. The paired construction changes how representations are obtained rather than simply adding another discriminative penalty to an existing sparse-coding pipeline.

The reported experiments cover a variety of visual classification tasks. The authors find substantially lower training and testing complexity alongside competitive classification accuracy. The abstract does not name the benchmarks or quantify those improvements, so it supports a speed-and-accuracy tradeoff within the evaluated tasks rather than a universal superiority claim over dictionary learning.

neurips-2015-are-you-talking-to-a-machin.tldr: An image-question answering model combines visual and language networks and is evaluated by human judges.
paragraphs: The paper addresses answering natural-language questions about images, with answers ranging from one word to a sentence. Its mQA model combines an LSTM for representing the question, a CNN for visual content, another LSTM for the answer’s linguistic context, and a fusion component that generates the answer.

The authors also construct FM-IQA, containing over 150,000 images and 310,000 freestyle Chinese question-answer pairs with English translations. To evaluate answer quality, they mix human and model responses and ask judges both to identify the source and to assign a quality score of 0, 1, or 2.

Judges cannot distinguish model answers from human answers in 64.7% of cases. The model receives an average quality score of 1.454, compared with 1.918 for humans. These results describe performance under this dataset and evaluation procedure; the remaining score gap matters even when a response’s source is difficult to identify.

neurips-2015-efficient-and-robust-automa.tldr: Auto-sklearn combines Bayesian optimization, experience from prior datasets, and ensembles.
paragraphs: An automated machine-learning system must choose preprocessing steps, a learning algorithm, and their hyperparameters for a new dataset. The paper introduces auto-sklearn, a scikit-learn-based system whose search space contains 15 classifiers, 14 feature-preprocessing methods, 4 data-preprocessing methods, and 110 hyperparameters.

The system extends Bayesian-optimization-based AutoML in two ways. It uses past performance on similar datasets to inform the search, and it constructs ensembles from models that the optimization has already evaluated. Thus, previously gathered experience guides exploration while evaluated candidates can contribute jointly to the final predictor.

Auto-sklearn won the first phase of the then-ongoing ChaLearn AutoML challenge. Evaluation on over 100 diverse datasets reports substantial improvements over the previous AutoML state of the art, with analyses separating the gains from individual contributions. The abstract provides broad comparative evidence, although it does not give per-dataset scores or resource budgets.

neurips-2015-gradient-free-hamiltonian-m.tldr: Kernel Hamiltonian Monte Carlo learns gradient structure to sample without target gradients.
paragraphs: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo can explore probability distributions efficiently, but it normally needs gradients of the target density. Those gradients can be intractable in some inference problems. This paper proposes Kernel Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, or KMC, to retain useful HMC-like behavior when direct gradient access is unavailable.

KMC adaptively fits an exponential-family model in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space to learn the target’s gradient structure. Two efficient approximations reduce the cost of using this learned structure. The resulting algorithm is gradient-free with respect to the target and is described as asymptotically exact.

Experiments on toy and real-world problems, including Approximate Bayesian Computation and exact-approximate MCMC, report substantial mixing improvements over other gradient-free samplers. The asymptotic claim concerns eventual correctness, while the experiments address sampling efficiency. The abstract does not supply finite-run error guarantees or numerical speedups for particular applications.

neurips-2015-lifted-inference-rules-with.tldr: A more expressive constraint language lets lifted inference exploit relational symmetries.
paragraphs: Lifted inference speeds up reasoning in statistical relational models by exploiting repeated structure and symmetries. Whether an inference rule is computationally useful depends strongly on how constraints over logical variables are represented. A restrictive representation can prevent the algorithm from expressing useful groups of equivalent substitutions.

The paper introduces setineq, a constraint language with subset, equality, and inequality constraints. It represents substitutions over variables and is claimed to be strictly more expressive than existing representations while remaining easy to manipulate. The authors reformulate the decomposer, generalized binomial, and single-occurrence lifting rules for this language, including the latter rule’s use in MAP inference.

Experiments on benchmark Markov logic networks evaluate exact and sampling-based inference and demonstrate advantages over several existing techniques. No numerical gains are given in the abstract. The contribution centers on representation and inference rules, with empirical support that additional expressiveness can translate into practical reasoning improvements.

neurips-2015-weakly-supervised-disentang.tldr: A recurrent encoder-decoder generates rotated object views from a single image.
paragraphs: Inferring an object’s appearance from a new viewpoint is ambiguous because a single image hides parts of its three-dimensional shape. This paper tackles the problem within object classes for which ample training data are available, specifically faces and chairs, rather than claiming unrestricted reconstruction from any photograph.

The proposed model is a recurrent convolutional encoder-decoder trained end to end to render rotated objects starting from one image. Its recurrent structure represents sequences of transformations and captures dependencies across those transformations. The learning setup also aims to separate underlying factors in its latent representation.

The authors demonstrate generated views on human faces from Multi-PIE and on a dataset of three-dimensional chair models. They additionally report disentangling latent factors without object-class labels. The abstract offers qualitative claims about prediction quality but no numerical comparison. The work connects view synthesis with learning representations whose factors can support controlled changes in appearance.

neurips-2016-a-credit-assignment-compile.tldr: A credit-assignment compiler makes learning-to-search systems easier and faster to implement.
paragraphs: Joint prediction tasks require several outputs to be chosen together because their values depend on one another. Learning to search handles this by turning a structured prediction into a sequence of decisions. Although the approach has theoretical and practical promise, defining the necessary search machinery has made implementations cumbersome.

This paper allows the search space to be specified by an arbitrary imperative program. The surrounding learning system becomes a credit-assignment compiler that supports learning over the program’s decisions. Algorithmic improvements to that compiler aim to reduce both execution cost and the amount of programming required.

Evaluations on multiple joint-prediction tasks obtain accuracy comparable to alternative approaches while substantially reducing programming and execution time. The abstract does not identify exact tasks, runtimes, or code-size measurements. The practical contribution is a programming interface and learning mechanism that make structured decision problems easier to express without sacrificing the reported predictive performance.

neurips-2016-an-efficient-streaming-algo.tldr: Partial coverage makes streaming submodular cover feasible despite a full-cover impossibility result.
paragraphs: The submodular cover problem seeks a collection whose combined value meets a coverage requirement. The paper asks what remains possible when data arrive as a stream and memory is smaller than the stream itself. It proves that a single-pass algorithm with sublinear memory cannot obtain any nontrivial approximation guarantee for the original streaming problem.

The authors therefore relax the objective to partial coverage and introduce ESC-Streaming, an efficient bicriteria algorithm. This changes the requirements in a way that permits theoretical performance guarantees while keeping the operational advantage of processing the stream only once.

Numerical evaluations consider active-set selection and large-scale graph cover. The resulting solutions are competitive with a near-optimal offline greedy algorithm. The distinction between full and partial cover is essential: the constructive result addresses the relaxed problem and does not overturn the impossibility theorem for the original formulation.

neurips-2016-bayesian-optimization-with-.tldr: Rollout approximations make Bayesian optimization account for a fixed evaluation budget.
paragraphs: When each evaluation of an objective is expensive, choosing where to sample depends on how many evaluations remain. This paper studies Bayesian optimization with a prescribed finite budget, treating the entire sequence of future sampling decisions as part of the optimization problem rather than considering only the next query.

The optimal strategy can be expressed through dynamic programming, but its state space is uncountable and grows in dimension, and its control space is also uncountable. The authors approximate this difficult planning problem with rollout and develop rollout heuristics tailored to Bayesian optimization.

Numerical experiments show that the resulting finite-budget optimizer outperforms several popular Bayesian-optimization algorithms. The abstract does not identify the tested objectives or report effect sizes, and the method is an approximation rather than an exact solution of the full dynamic program. Its main contribution is a practical route toward budget-aware planning of costly experiments.

neurips-2016-learning-sensor-multiplexin.tldr: Jointly learning a camera’s color sampling pattern and reconstruction network improves color imaging.
paragraphs: A typical color-camera sensor measures only one color channel at each pixel, so software must reconstruct the missing channels. The usual learning pipeline takes that sensor layout as fixed. This paper extends backpropagation into the measurement process so that the color sampling pattern and reconstruction network can be learned together.

The sensor is represented as a layer whose trainable weights determine which channel, from a fixed set, is measured at each position. These weights are optimized jointly with a network that converts the resulting measurements into a full-color image. The design objective therefore links physical sampling choices to reconstruction accuracy.

The reported network improves accuracy substantially over the traditional Bayer pattern. It also learns sparse color measurements resembling a recent design and improves that design’s spatial layout. The abstract concerns this specific color-multiplexing setting; it does not establish improvements for every camera component or imaging task.

neurips-2016-multi-step-learning-and-und.tldr: A statistical framework identifies conditions under which intermediate learning steps reduce sample needs.
paragraphs: Multi-step learning assumes that intermediate tasks transform data into representations useful for a final task. This paper asks when that intuition produces a real statistical advantage. It includes semi-supervised learning, where an unsupervised step precedes supervised learning, within a broader generative description of learning problems.

The authors define a joint statistical model over inputs and outputs. For each input marginal, this specifies compatible conditional distributions, giving an abstract compatibility relation between unlabeled data and the prediction task. They introduce gamma-uniform shattering as a tool for analyzing both discrete and nondiscrete statistical models.

Theoretical conditions on marginal and conditional models establish advantages for multi-step learning. One result generalizes an earlier invariance result: under mild hypotheses, learning features invariant to successive factors of a finite group has sample complexity additive rather than multiplicative in subgroup sizes. These gains depend on model structure and assumptions, rather than holding for arbitrary preprocessing sequences.

neurips-2016-on-multiplicative-integrati.tldr: Multiplicative Integration changes recurrent-network information combination with almost no extra parameters.
paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks repeatedly combine information inside a computational building block. The paper investigates whether changing that integration mechanism can improve learning without substantially increasing model size. It introduces a structural design called Multiplicative Integration, or MI, intended as a small modification to existing recurrent architectures.

MI changes how information flows are combined in the recurrent computation while adding almost no parameters. The design can be embedded in popular architectures, including LSTMs and GRUs. This makes it a reusable modification to the recurrent building block rather than an entirely separate task-specific model.

The authors analyze learning behavior empirically and evaluate multiple recurrent models across several tasks. They report substantial performance improvements over many existing recurrent-network models. The abstract does not specify the tasks, numerical gains, or detailed integration formula, so those claims should be read at the level of the evaluated comparisons. Its central contribution is a lightweight architectural change with broad reported empirical benefits.

neurips-2016-solving-marginal-map-proble.tldr: XOR MMAP reduces difficult marginal-MAP inference to optimization with parity constraints.
paragraphs: Marginal MAP combines choosing the best decision with summing over uncertain variables. These maximization and counting requirements make it more difficult than either inference task on its own. The paper proposes XOR MMAP for applications where decision-making and probabilistic inference must be solved together.

The approach represents the intractable counting component using queries to NP oracles with added parity constraints. It encodes the marginal-MAP task as a single optimization problem whose size is polynomial in the original problem, and provides a constant-factor approximation guarantee.

Experiments on several machine-learning and decision-making applications show improvements over multiple state-of-the-art marginal-MAP solvers. The abstract does not name the application instances or report runtimes. The theoretical reduction is not a claim that every resulting optimization is easy; its value is connecting a harder combined inference problem to an oracle-based formulation with an explicit approximation guarantee.

neurips-2017-adaptive-stimulus-selection.tldr: Adept selects images adaptively to elicit stronger and more varied population neural responses.
paragraphs: A stimulus that strongly activates one neuron may not be useful for an entire recorded population. This paper develops Adept, an adaptive selection method that optimizes objectives involving responses across multiple neurons. The goal is to support experiments where useful stimuli are difficult to identify in advance.

Simulations first show that population objectives elicit more diverse responses than single-neuron objectives. The authors then test Adept in closed-loop electrophysiology in macaque V4, using deep-convolutional-network outputs as feature embeddings for predicting neural responses and selecting images.

Images chosen by Adept produce mean neural responses 20% larger than randomly selected natural images and evoke greater response diversity. These findings support the approach in the tested population and stimulus setting. They do not imply that one image maximizes every neuron simultaneously; the method explicitly targets an objective that evaluates the recorded population together.

neurips-2017-attention-is-all-you-need-3.tldr: An attention-only sequence architecture improves translation quality while allowing more parallel computation.
paragraphs: Sequence-transduction systems commonly used recurrent or convolutional encoders and decoders, often with attention connecting them. This paper proposes an architecture built solely around attention, removing recurrence and convolutions from the model. The motivation is to improve translation while allowing more computation to proceed in parallel.

The authors evaluate the architecture on two machine-translation tasks and report better quality with substantially less training time. Their supplied abstract describes a single model with 165 million parameters achieving 27.5 BLEU on English-to-German translation, more than 1 BLEU above the previous best ensemble result.

For English-to-French translation, the abstract reports 41.1 BLEU, exceeding the previous best single-model result by 0.7 BLEU. These are the figures stated in this source abstract. The evidence concerns the two translation tasks, and the abstract does not provide a detailed architectural breakdown or establish performance across all sequence-learning applications.

neurips-2017-deep-reinforcement-learning.tldr: Human comparisons of short behavior segments can train reinforcement-learning goals with sparse feedback.
paragraphs: Complex goals can be difficult to communicate as an explicit reward function. This paper instead asks nonexpert humans to compare pairs of short trajectory segments. It separates learning what behavior people prefer from learning a policy that achieves the inferred goal.

The approach is tested on Atari games and simulated robot locomotion without giving the learner access to the task’s reward function. Human feedback covers about 0.1% of the agent’s interactions with its environment, showing that direct supervision of every action is unnecessary in these experiments.

The authors also report training complex novel behaviors with about an hour of human time. This supports the flexibility and practical feasibility of preference-based goal learning in the evaluated environments. It does not mean all real-world goals can be inferred from that amount of feedback; the abstract’s evidence is tied to these demonstrations and their particular human-comparison setup.

neurips-2017-learning-overcomplete-hmms-.tldr: Structural assumptions determine when hidden Markov models with many hidden states can be learned.
paragraphs: An overcomplete hidden Markov model has many hidden states but only a small alphabet of observable outputs. That mismatch makes learning difficult because many internal configurations must be inferred from limited observable symbols. The paper develops positive and negative results that distinguish tractable cases from settings where data are insufficient.

The positive results apply to a large subclass whose transition matrices are sparse, well-conditioned, and assign little probability mass to short cycles. These structural requirements are part of the learning guarantee and cannot be dropped when interpreting the result.

Conversely, the authors show that a polynomial number of samples cannot suffice for certain models with small output alphabets and transition matrices formed by high-degree random regular graphs. They discuss implications for modeling long-term dependencies. The contribution is a map of learnability boundaries, rather than a single algorithm claimed to handle all overcomplete hidden Markov models.

neurips-2017-on-optimal-generalizability.tldr: Approximate leave-one-out validation makes regularizer selection more computationally practical.
paragraphs: Parameters fitted by empirical risk minimization are influenced by their training data, so their performance must be assessed out of sample. Leave-one-out cross-validation repeatedly trains on every sample except one, but the repeated fitting makes it expensive. This paper develops a computationally efficient approximation to that procedure.

The proposed approximate leave-one-out cross-validation method, ALOOCV, comes with theoretical performance guarantees. The authors then use it within an optimization algorithm for choosing the regularizer in empirical risk minimization, connecting efficient performance estimation to the design of the fitted model.

Numerical experiments illustrate both the accuracy and efficiency of the approximation and the usefulness of regularizer optimization. The abstract supplies no specific datasets, speedups, or approximation-error values. Its contribution is the combination of a justified validation approximation and a method that uses that approximation to tune regularization, rather than an assertion that validation is unnecessary.

neurips-2018-a-unified-feature-disentang.tldr: A shared disentangled representation supports image translation, manipulation, and domain adaptation.
paragraphs: Images from different domains contain both shared information and domain-specific variation. This paper aims to learn a representation that captures what remains consistent across domains while still using information unique to each domain. The intended payoff is one framework that supports several cross-domain image tasks.

The proposed deep network uses adversarial training to learn domain-invariant representations and includes a mechanism for exploiting domain-specific information. It can perform continuous image translation and manipulation across multiple domains, producing outputs that reflect the requested changes.

The authors also evaluate the learned features for unsupervised domain adaptation and report superior performance, which they interpret as evidence of effective feature disentanglement. The abstract does not name datasets, metrics, or comparison methods, so the strength of that evidence cannot be quantified here. The work’s scope is a unified representation-learning approach evaluated through both image generation and transfer of learned features.

neurips-2018-empirical-risk-minimization.tldr: Polynomial approximation improves noninteractive private learning under smoothness and structural assumptions.
paragraphs: This paper studies empirical risk minimization when each participant privately reports information without interactive rounds. The central issue is how sample requirements and computation depend on dimension, accuracy, and the structure of the loss. The authors treat low-dimensional and high-dimensional regimes separately.

For constant or low dimension and an infinitely smooth loss with the stated smoothness condition, polynomial approximation avoids a sample-complexity dependence of the form alpha to the power minus p. They also obtain participant-efficient algorithms requiring one bit of communication and constant computation per participant, with asymptotically matching error bounds. Efficient server computation needs additional assumptions.

In high dimensions, convex generalized linear losses permit error bounds involving the Gaussian width of the constraint set instead of ambient dimension p. These are assumption-dependent theoretical improvements. The abstract does not claim the same guarantees for arbitrary losses or arbitrary constraint sets, and it provides no empirical benchmark results.

neurips-2018-learning-attentional-commun.tldr: Learned attention decides when agents should communicate and how shared information should influence actions.
paragraphs: Communication can help cooperative agents, but broadcasting everything becomes problematic as the group grows. Useful information can be buried in irrelevant messages, while a fixed communication architecture can prevent helpful exchanges. This paper addresses both issues by learning how communication should support decisions.

The proposed attentional communication model learns when communication is needed and how to integrate the information that is shared. Its aim is efficient, effective cooperation among many agents, with communication adapted to the task rather than uniformly available or restricted by a predefined pattern.

Experiments span multiple cooperative scenarios and show agents developing more coordinated and sophisticated strategies than existing methods. The abstract does not specify agent counts, communication costs, or quantitative improvements. The supported conclusion is that learned selection and integration of messages improve cooperation in the tested settings; it is not a guarantee for every large multi-agent system.
